covers.quote: Write official names with capitals
Some shortened forms that are popular names or nicknames are also capitalised.

examples.note: Initial capitals on full feature name

parts.quote: the Hunter Valley

examples.note: Initial capitals on full feature name

parts.quote: the Three Sisters

examples.note: Initial capitals on full feature name

parts.quote: the Paroo River
The Snowy Mountains can also be called the ‘Snowies’.
The northern part of the Northern Territory is known as the ‘Top End’.

rules.quote: The full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other features always take initial capitals.
rules.violation_condition: a full topographic feature name written without initial capitals
when: applies to official full names of landmark features, mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other topographic features
some popular shortened names or nicknames are also capitalised (e.g. the 'Snowies', the 'Top End')
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Heading 738bf9ea92fc is specified by e6faa2dc7159 and extended to nicknames by 39ae94927f5a.

covers.quote: Write generic terms in lower case
When using the same generic term for 2 or more names in the same sentence, use lower case for the generic term.
Keep the initial capital when the general term is a well-recognised abbreviation and works as a proper name.
Don’t use an initial capital if you’re using the noun in a generic sense.

examples.note: 'The river' uses lower case for generic reference

parts.quote: I paddled a kayak 200 km down the Balonne River. The river was in flood for some of the trip.

examples.note: Shared generic term in lower case

parts.quote: The Barossa and Hunter valleys are important winemaking areas.
The Barossa Valley is in South Australia and the Hunter Valley is in New South Wales.
The Great Barrier Reef is also called ‘the Reef’.
The Gulf of Carpentaria is also known as ‘the Gulf’.
The Amazon rainforest is vital to the health of our planet.

rules.quote: In most cases, don’t use initial capitals when you use the name as a generic term.
rules.violation_condition: a generic topographic term written with an initial capital
when: applies when referring to a topographic feature generically (e.g. 'the river')
applies when using the same generic term for 2 or more names in the same sentence (e.g. 'the Barossa and Hunter valleys')
does not apply when the general term is a well-recognised abbreviation that works as a proper name (e.g. 'the Reef', 'the Gulf')
rules.why: G-1, G-2, G-4: The heading and sub-rules describe the same rule regarding generic vs proper terms, consolidated into one rule with conditions/exceptions.

covers.quote: Limit abbreviated names
‘Mt’is a common and easily recognisable abbreviation for mountains. Use the abbreviation consistently in content and use initial capitals.
Use Geoscience Australia’s authorised abbreviations.

parts.quote: Mt Tennent is part of Namadgi National Park.
C Tribulation
L Burley Griffin
Murray R
Green Is
Keppel Bay Is

rules.quote: Spell out the names of other topographic features if you can. Use the abbreviated form only where there’s limited space or a lot of repetition, such as in tables and maps.
rules.specification: Topographic terms other than 'Mt' should be spelled out in full in running prose, reserving abbreviations for tables, maps, or tightly space-constrained contexts.
rules.violation_condition: an abbreviated topographic feature name used in running text where space is not constrained
when: 'Mt' is accepted as a common abbreviation for mountain and may be used in content
other abbreviations may be used where space is limited or there is repetitive listing, such as tables and maps
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Heading 4931f9c057a3 and supporting paragraphs govern abbreviating topographic features and the exception for 'Mt'.

covers.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe for possessive names

parts.quote: Careys Peak
Carey’s Peak

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe for topographic terms involving possessives.
rules.violation_condition: an apostrophe in a topographic place name (e.g. Carey's Peak)
rules.why: G-4: Rule stated in heading and body; body sentence marked with direct matching example pair.

covers.quote: Spell the plural form correctly

parts.quote: There are 4 Mount Wellingtons in Australia but only one Mount Coot-tha.
There are 3 Mount Jameses in Australia. There is one in Queensland, one in South Australia and one in Western Australia.

rules.quote: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
rules.violation_condition: a plural topographic name formed with an apostrophe or irregular inflection rather than adding 's' or 'es'
rules.why: G-1, G-4: Heading is generic advice/label, body sentence provides actionable specification.

covers.quote: Write compass points in lower case
You can use initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works. Always use capital letters with no full stops or hyphens.

parts.quote: south

examples.note: Lower case hyphenated compound compass point

parts.quote: north-east

examples.note: Lower case hyphenated compound compass point

parts.quote: west-north-west
A north-westerly wind was blowing the fire towards the town.
The car was 30 degrees east of where it should have been.
A cool change was coming from the south.

rules.quote: In text, write the points of a compass in lower case. Use hyphens for points such as ‘north-east’.
rules.violation_condition: a compass point written in text with capital letters or without a hyphen for compound points (e.g. 'North-East' or 'northeast')
when: initialisms (all capital letters without full stops or hyphens) can be used in tables, illustrations and specialist works
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Heading is consolidated with text sentence and its exception for initialisms in illustrations/tables.
